name: Saw palmetto (Serenoa repens)
short: Isolated reports of death and brain bleeding (causality questionable); case reports of surgical bleeding, pancreatitis, liver injury. Trials in men with prostate enlargement: mild, like placebo.
text: A systematic review of human safety data on saw palmetto single-ingredient preparations (40 articles, including 26 randomized controlled trials and 4 case reports or series) found adverse events mild and similar to those with placebo, most often abdominal pain, diarrhoea, nausea, fatigue, headache, decreased libido and rhinitis; more serious adverse events such as death and cerebral haemorrhage were reported in isolated case reports and spontaneous reporting data, but the reviewers judged causality questionable, and they found no evidence of drug interactions. An updated Cochrane review of 17 randomised placebo-controlled trials (2,008 men with benign prostatic hyperplasia, 4 to 72 weeks) likewise found adverse events few and mild and not significantly different from placebo, and a 1-year placebo-controlled trial in 225 men with benign prostatic hyperplasia found no significant difference in serious adverse events (5.4% with saw palmetto vs 9.7% with placebo), while noting that its size and length could not rule out rare adverse effects. On bleeding and surgery, case reports describe severe bleeding during surgery in a man taking saw palmetto, whose prolonged bleeding time normalised a few days after he stopped the herb, and blood in the urine with a clotting abnormality in another user; in contrast, a randomized trial in 75 men having prostate surgery (transurethral resection) found no significant difference in blood loss after 5 weeks of saw palmetto compared with a control group, a randomized trial in 144 men having prostate surgery reported fewer intraoperative complications and transfusions after 2 months of saw palmetto than with no pre-treatment, and a review of dietary supplements and bleeding concluded that saw palmetto is not associated with bleeding. Other case reports describe acute hepatitis and pancreatitis in a 55-year-old man that improved on withdrawal and recurred twice when saw palmetto was restarted, and cholestatic drug-induced liver injury in a 70-year-old man, in which the authors said causality could not be definitively established because of exposure to other drugs but considered saw palmetto the most likely agent, based on the timing of exposure, exclusion of other causes, compatible liver biopsy findings and improvement after it was stopped. No interaction data were found in the cited sources beyond the systematic review's finding of no reported drug interactions.
